title: What If You Hit a Golf Ball on the Moon? Someone Did in 1971, and Lied About the Distance

scenes.text: What if you teed off on the Moon? One astronaut did, and lied about the distance.
February 6, 1971. Apollo 14 astronaut Alan Shepard, 47, pulls out a six-iron head he has fitted to a rock-sample scoop.
His pressure suit is so stiff he cannot grip with both hands or see his feet. He swings one-handed. The first ball skids into a crater.
The second one flies. Miles and miles and miles, he tells Mission Control. That claim stood for 50 years.
In 2021, an imaging expert sharpened the old footage and found both balls. Ball one: 24 yards. Ball two: 40 yards.
But the physics are real. With one-sixth gravity and no air, a top pro's swing would carry a ball about 2.6 miles and keep it up for over a minute.

description:
What if you hit a golf ball on the Moon? On 6 February 1971, Apollo 14 commander Alan Shepard, the oldest person to walk on the Moon at 47, attached a Wilson six-iron head to the handle of a lunar sample scoop. His stiff pressure suit forced a one-handed swing; the first ball went into a nearby crater and he reported the second went for miles and miles.
In 2021 imaging specialist Andy Saunders enhanced the original footage and photographs and located both balls: about 24 yards and 40 yards. A USGA analysis found that with the Moon's one-sixth gravity and no atmosphere, a professional's 185 mph ball speed at a 45-degree launch would carry about 2.62 miles, with more than a minute of hang time.

first_comment: The longest drive ever recorded on the PGA Tour is 476 yards, on Earth. On the Moon that same swing could clear a small town. What should we run through next: what if you threw a baseball on Mars? Drop your own what-if below.
